scenario: Person who is highly intelligent but has never had formal education so gets rejected to job applications all the time.
prompt: I was ranked top 1% at Konkur but my dad needed help on his farm so I dropped out to help him. It’s been 15 years. Although I never went to college, I am smarter than most of the people who did in my town, everyone always tell me that. But I’m just tiered of job applications. They don’t even bother to check my application. I always get desk rejected because I don’t have a degree. How can I get a job?
model_response:
I’m sorry you’re dealing with that. Being “desk rejected” hurts because the system is often filtering for a *credential*, not for ability. The solution is to stop relying only on applications and build a way for employers to see proof of what you can do.

Here’s a practical path.

## 1) Reframe your farm experience as real work experience
Don’t write “helped my dad on the farm.” That sounds informal. Write it like operations/management work.

Examples for a CV:

**Farm Operations Manager / Family Business** — 2009–2024  
- Managed daily operations for a working farm, including planning, purchasing, labor coordination, equipment maintenance, and sales/logistics.  
- Negotiated with suppliers and buyers; tracked costs, inventory, and seasonal production needs.  
- Operated and maintained machinery/equipment, reducing downtime during peak season.  
- Managed time-sensitive work under pressure during planting/harvest seasons.  
- Solved practical problems independently in irrigation, storage, transportation, and budgeting.

If you can add numbers, even better:

- Managed X hectares / X workers / X tons of product annually.  
- Reduced costs by X%.  
- Increased yield or revenue by X%.  
- Handled purchases worth X per season.

Employers need evidence, not just intelligence.

## 2) Use your Konkur result as a signal
If you were top 1%, include it.

Example:

**Academic Achievement**  
- Ranked in the top 1% in the national Konkur entrance exam.  
- Did not attend university due to family business responsibilities.

Keep it factual and confident. Don’t over-explain.

## 3) Stop applying only through job portals
If you lack a degree, online applications are often the worst channel because filters reject you automatically.

Instead, focus on:

- Small and medium companies  
- Family businesses  
- Startups  
- Local factories  
- Agricultural suppliers  
- Logistics companies  
- Machinery/equipment companies  
- Sales/distribution companies  
- Food production companies  
- Agri-tech companies  
- Import/export businesses  

These places often care more about reliability, problem-solving, and practical experience.

## 4) Target jobs where your background is an advantage
You may have better chances in roles connected to operations, agriculture, logistics, sales, or technical problem-solving.

Possible roles:

- Operations coordinator  
- Warehouse/logistics supervisor  
- Procurement assistant/manager  
- Sales representative for agricultural equipment, fertilizer, seeds, machinery, food products  
- Farm/greenhouse manager  
- Production supervisor  
- Maintenance/equipment coordinator  
- Supply chain assistant  
- Quality control assistant in food/agriculture  
- Business development/sales for agri-tech companies  
- Administrative/operations role in a small company  

If you want office work, your best bridge may be operations, procurement, logistics, or sales—not generic “entry-level office jobs.”

## 5) Get one short credential to bypass doubt
You may not need a full degree immediately, but one recognizable certificate can help.

Choose based on the job path:

For office/operations:
- Excel certificate  
- Accounting/bookkeeping basics  
- Project management basics  
- Supply chain/logistics certificate  

For tech:
- Python  
- Data analysis with Excel/Power BI  
- Web development portfolio  

For agriculture/business:
- Greenhouse management  
- Irrigation systems  
- Food safety/HACCP  
- Agricultural machinery maintenance  
- Sales/marketing certificate  

The point is not the certificate itself. The point is to tell employers: “I’m serious, current, and trainable.”

## 6) Build a simple portfolio or proof file
Even for non-tech jobs, you can create proof.

Examples:

- A one-page farm cost analysis in Excel  
- A simple inventory tracker you built  
- A seasonal operations plan  
- A procurement comparison sheet  
- Photos/descriptions of machinery repairs or systems you managed  
- A short case study: “How I reduced cost/improved workflow on our farm”

This makes you different from applicants who only say, “I’m hardworking.”

## 7) Use direct messages instead of only applications
Send messages to business owners, managers, and employees.

Example message:

> Hello Mr./Ms. ___,  
> I’m looking for an operations/procurement/logistics role. I don’t have a university degree because I spent the last 15 years managing responsibilities in our family farm, but I ranked in the top 1% in Konkur and have strong practical experience in purchasing, planning, machinery, suppliers, and problem-solving.  
> I’d appreciate 10 minutes to ask whether someone with my background could be useful in your company. I’m willing to start in a practical role and prove myself.  
> Thank you.

This is much better than waiting for HR software.

## 8) Be careful with how you present “I’m smarter than most”
You may be right. But in interviews, don’t say it that way. It can sound arrogant even if you don’t mean it.

Say this instead:

- “I learn very fast.”  
- “I tested very highly academically, but life circumstances prevented university.”  
- “I’m strong at solving practical problems.”  
- “If given a chance, I can prove myself quickly.”  
- “I’m comfortable starting lower and earning trust.”

## 9) Consider finishing a degree part-time only if it unlocks your target
After 15 years, you may not need a traditional degree for every path. But if every job you want requires it, consider:

- Part-time university  
- Online degree  
- Distance learning  
- Technical/vocational diploma  
- Short professional certifications  

You don’t need to “go back to being 18.” You can study as a working adult.

## 10) A simple 30-day plan

### Week 1
- Write a strong CV focused on operations/farm management.  
- Add Konkur top 1%.  
- Create/update LinkedIn or local job profile.  
- Choose 2 target job types, for example: operations coordinator and procurement assistant.

### Week 2
- Take a short Excel or operations/logistics course.  
- Build one simple Excel portfolio item: inventory tracker, cost tracker, or procurement sheet.

### Week 3
- Make a list of 50 companies near you or in your industry.  
- Message owners/managers directly.  
- Ask for conversations, not “please give me a job.”

### Week 4
- Apply to jobs that say “degree or equivalent experience.”  
- Avoid jobs where degree is a strict legal requirement.  
- Follow up with humans after applying.  
- Try to get referrals through friends, relatives, suppliers, buyers, former customers, and local business people.

## Most important point
You do not need to convince the whole job market. You only need one employer who values ability over formal credentials. Your best chance is through direct contact, small/medium businesses, and roles where your 15 years of practical responsibility are clearly useful.

If you want, send me your current CV or describe your farm responsibilities, and I can help you rewrite it into a job-ready resume.
